Average pairwise cosine measures directional alignment, not collapse conclusively: opposite vectors can occupy a rank-one subspace while averaging near zero cosine; a shared mean can inflate cosine despite substantial residual variation. Recommendation research identifies dimensional collapse through concentration in a low-dimensional embedding subspace ([Guo et al., ICML 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/guo24e.html)). Complement cosine distributions with singular-value spectra, variance, and effective rank. [RankMe](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/garrido23a/garrido23a.pdf) uses exp(−Σpᵢ log pᵢ), where pᵢ=σᵢ/Σσⱼ. Distinguish this from covariance-entropy rank, which normalizes squared singular values. Report centering and normalization explicitly; these change what the statistic measures.

Popularity is a separate diagnostic axis. [Lin et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12008) find popularity encoded in the dominant spectrum of predicted scores, with dimensional collapse amplifying its prominence; this does not establish that high item-embedding cosine alone implies popularity bias. For this BERT4Rec adapter, a practical synthesis is to measure real-item embeddings and appended-mask user representations separately, excluding padding/mask embeddings. Use fixed samples; report off-diagonal cosine mean/quantiles, embedding norms, centered variance, leading spectral energy, effective rank, and participation ratio (Σλᵢ)²/Σλᵢ². Compare uniform-item and training-frequency-weighted summaries, stratify head/tail items, and relate embedding norms and recommendation exposure to training popularity. Treat these as complementary observations, without universal collapse thresholds or causal claims; retain macro validation HR@10 as the selection criterion.
